alalal-e84681-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 21: whether believing, the act of faith, naturally precedes hoping.

alalal-e84681-d1e115.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's statement in the last chapter that believing naturally precedes hoping, and notes contrary authorities.

alalal-e84681-d1e131.summary: First objection: the Gloss on Psalm 36:1 says hope is the entrance to faith.

alalal-e84681-d1e144.summary: Second objection: charity is the mother and form of all virtues, as Lombard also says, so faith is not first.

alalal-e84681-d1e157.summary: Third objection: whoever has one virtue has all, so none is prior.

alalal-e84681-d1e164.summary: Fourth objection: withdrawing from evil precedes doing good; fear withdraws from evil, faith approaches the true good, so fear is first.

alalal-e84681-d1e180.summary: Fifth objection: Ecclesiasticus 1:27 says fear of the Lord drives out sin, and without fear no one can be justified.

alalal-e84681-d1e191.summary: Solution: faith or its act naturally precedes, as Lombard says, since fear will not flee evil unless faith shows it, nor love desire the good unless faith shows it. Though simultaneous in time, faith is prior by nature, being in reason before a person's movement toward justice.
claims: Faith is naturally prior to the other virtues, since it shows the evil fear flees and the good love seeks.

alalal-e84681-d1e215.summary: Considering justification as a motion with a terminus from which and to which: relative to the terminus from which, sin ordered to punishment, fear is the first mover; relative to the terminus to which, hope first disposes the mobile, raising it by the expectation of pardon, and love is the first mover. So different virtues can be first in justification, but faith is always naturally prior to all, since in the order of understanding it precedes the whole motion, showing from what, to what and how one moves.
claims: In justification fear is first regarding sin, hope disposes and love moves toward the end, but faith precedes the whole motion by showing its terms.
concepts: terminus a quo and ad quem

alalal-e84681-d1e264.summary: This answers all except the Gloss on Psalm 36: there 'faith' means not the habit by which one believes but what is believed, the eternal good, into which hope leads as expectation of eternal good.

alalal-e84681.summary: Article 21 defends Lombard's statement that believing naturally precedes hoping, against authorities giving priority to hope, charity or fear. Albert holds that although the virtues are simultaneous in time, faith is prior by nature: fear would not flee evil, nor love seek the good, unless faith showed them. Considered as a motion, justification has fear as first mover away from sin, hope as disposing toward pardon and love as first mover toward the end. Faith still precedes the whole motion, because it shows its starting point, goal and manner. The Gloss calling hope the entrance to faith takes 'faith' as the eternal good believed in.
claims: Faith is naturally prior to hope and the other virtues, though they are simultaneous in time.
In justification fear, hope and love are each first in some respect, but faith precedes the whole motion.
